questions.heading: Rounding Up, or to the Nearest Whole, Can Break the Budget
questions.stem: A district's LP relaxation funds projects R1 and R2 whole and 0.6 of R3, and spends its budget of 900 exactly. R3 costs 250. What does rounding to the nearest whole give?

options.text: A plan spending 900, since rounding moves spend up and down equally
options.says: Nothing is rounded down here: R1 and R2 are already whole, and R3's 0.6 goes up, so spend only rises.

options.text: A plan spending 1,000, since the 0.4 of R3 left unpaid is now paid
options.says: Right: R3 rounds up, and its missing 0.4 x 250 = 100 lands on a budget the LP had already spent.

options.text: A plan spending 750, since the 0.6 of R3 the LP funded is dropped
options.says: That is rounding down; 0.6 is at least 0.5, so the nearest whole is 1.

options.text: A plan spending 1,150, since all of R3's cost is added to the LP's spend
options.says: The LP's 900 already includes 0.6 of R3; only the missing 0.4 is added.

questions.heading: Rounding Down Keeps This Model's Rows, and Still Misses the Best Plan
questions.stem: A route model must inspect at least 120 poles and minimizes cost. Its LP relaxation takes route U whole and 0.5 of route V. What goes wrong if the team rounds down?

options.text: The pole row is a maximum, so dropping half of V can exceed the poles allowed
options.says: The row says at least 120: it is a minimum, and dropping work can only lower the count.

options.text: The objective is minimized, so dropping half of V can raise the plan's cost
options.says: Costs are positive, so dropping a route lowers cost; the risk is in the row, not the objective.

options.text: The LP answer is fractional, so dropping half of V can leave no plan to report
options.says: Rounding down returns a 0/1 plan either way; the question is whether it keeps the rows.

options.text: The pole row is a minimum, so dropping half of V can leave poles uninspected
options.says: Right: lowering a variable can break a >= row, as the lesson's 400 km corridor example shows.

questions.heading: Rounding Down Then Filling Gives an Allowed Plan, Never a Proof
questions.stem: A fill heuristic returns an allowed plan worth 9,940. The LP relaxation's value is 10,000, and no MILP was solved. What can the team state about the plan?

options.text: It is at most 60 below the best plan, and it may be the best plan
options.says: Right: the LP value is a ceiling on every allowed plan, so the best is somewhere from 9,940 to 10,000.

options.text: It is exactly 60 below the best plan, since the LP value is a plan
options.says: The LP's answer is fractional, so its value is a ceiling, not the value of an allowed plan.

options.text: It is the best plan, since the model's rows allow it
options.says: Keeping the rows makes it allowed, not best; the lesson's filled plan was allowed and 46 short.

options.text: It is at least 60 below the best plan, since the LP value bounds it
options.says: The ceiling limits the shortfall from above: the plan is at most 60 short, possibly 0.
